cards.hook: Minimising your tax now can cost you a house later.
cards.so_what: Self-employed and buying within two years? Ask your accountant how your next return will read to a bank.

posts.linkedin:
Minimising your tax now can cost you a house later.

If you're self-employed or contracting, the instinct is to keep reported income as low as your accountant can get it. Fair enough, in most years.

But a lender only sees what's on your tax returns. If the plan is to buy in the next year or two, those returns are your borrowing capacity. A great year minimised down on paper becomes a smaller loan when you apply.

So if a purchase is on the horizon, build the returns with that in mind, with your accountant, so the income you actually earn is income a bank can use.

Self-employed and buying within two years? Ask your accountant how your next return will read to a bank.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.myth: Building a few townhouses means you need a private lender.
cards.reality: A first small project usually fits a normal construction loan.
cards.because: Two or three dwellings on reasonably priced land can often go mainstream. Same result, without a couple of percent extra in private rates and fees.

posts.linkedin:
Two or three townhouses? Don't pay private-lender prices.

A lot of people doing their first small development assume it's private money from the start. Higher rate, establishment fees, the lot. For bigger projects, sometimes that's right.

For a first, smaller one, two or three dwellings, we'd rather keep it in mainstream construction lending, provided the land price is reasonable. If you can get the same result while saving a couple of percent on rate and fees, there's no reason to pay for private money.

Before you go private, ask whether a mainstream construction loan can fund the project.

General information only, not personal advice.

cards.text:
Different banks win at different things.

The lender with the sharpest rate for your refinance often isn’t the one that will lend you the most for your next purchase.

So we might refinance you with one bank and fund the next purchase with another.

One bank for everything is tidy. Matching each loan to the bank that’s best at that job usually serves you better.

posts.linkedin:
Different banks win at different things. Use more than one.

Most people like the idea of one bank for everything. It's tidy. One app, one login, one relationship.

But lenders aren't equally good at everything. The one with the sharpest rate for a refinance is often not the one that will lend you the most for your next purchase.

So we'll sometimes refinance you with one lender for the rate, then use a different lender for the next purchase, where borrowing capacity matters more. Each loan goes to the bank that's strongest for that job.

Ask which lender is strongest for the job you need done now, not overall.

General information only, not personal advice.

#refinance #propertyinvestor #homeloan

cards.title: Houses usually grow faster
cards.body: If the budget stretches, a house beats a unit as an investment almost every time. In many family-oriented regional markets, renters want houses too.

cards.body: When borrowing capacity forces it, or it’s a genuinely exceptional deal. Otherwise, ask what a house in a proven area costs before you settle.

cards.body: A small town that just looks cheap may not grow at all. Thin markets have little data behind the price. The same budget often buys better somewhere proven.

cards.label: investing
cards.headline: House or unit? Proven or cheap?
cards.body: A 15-minute chat is enough to know where you stand.

posts.linkedin:
If you can afford it, buy the house.

That's our view on investment property, almost every time. Houses tend to grow faster in value, and in many family-oriented regional markets they're what renters are looking for too. A unit makes sense when borrowing capacity forces it, or when it's a genuinely exceptional deal.

The other trap we see: buying somewhere just because it's cheap. Small towns with little sales data are a real risk. You can't be sure they'll grow at all, and the same budget often buys a better property in a proven market.

Before you buy, ask what a house in a proven area costs versus the unit or cheap town you're looking at, and ask for the data.

General information only, not personal advice.

#propertyinvestor #investmentproperty #realestateaustralia
